expectations.text: Identifies the EBIC gamma (tuning) parameter as the primary lever for controlling network sparsity
expectations.evidence: Dedicated section 'Culprit 2: Gamma is too liberal — increase it' explains that gamma 'controls how aggressively the model penalizes edge inclusion' and provides explicit code stepping from tuning=0.5 to tuning=1.0.

expectations.text: States the field convention: default gamma = 0.5; recommend trying higher values (e.g., 0.5 → 1.0) to see how sparsity changes
expectations.evidence: 'gamma = 0.5 is the field default per Epskamp & Fried (2018)' and code examples explicitly show tuning = 0.5 vs tuning = 1.0 with a note that 0.75–1.0 are 'defensible and commonly used.'

expectations.text: Flags that Pearson correlations on ordinal Likert items can inflate edge weights — recommends checking that cor_auto or polychoric correlations are being used
expectations.evidence: cor_auto appears silently in all code snippets but the response never explicitly warns that using Pearson correlations on ordinal/Likert data inflates edge weights or explains why cor_auto matters for this use case.

expectations.text: Mentions node redundancy or near-duplicate items as a possible cause of dense networks (spuriously strong partial correlations that survive regularization)
expectations.evidence: 'Culprit 1: Node redundancy (check this first)' — 'items like sad mood, depressed affect, and feels empty have nearly identical conditioning sets… creating a cluster of very strong edges that then propagates spurious density throughout the graph.'

expectations.text: Does NOT conclude that a near-complete graph is acceptable without any action or investigation
expectations.evidence: Opens with '91 out of 105 edges (87% density) is pathologically dense… it's a clear signal that something upstream is wrong before you even get to interpretation' and provides an extensive remediation plan.
